section_1.title: Prerequisite Review: Determinants as Area
section_1.content: Define the determinant of a 2x2 matrix as the signed area of the parallelogram formed by its column vectors. Establish that a non-zero determinant implies the vectors are linearly independent, spanning a 2D space.
section_1.example: A parallelogram defined by vectors v1=(2,0) and v2=(0,2) has a determinant of 4, representing its area.

section_2.title: Visualizing the System Ax = b
section_2.content: Represent the system of linear equations as a vector combination: x(a1) + y(a2) = b. Geometrically, this means finding the scalar weights (x, y) that scale the column vectors a1 and a2 so that their diagonal sum lands exactly on the target vector b.
section_2.example: Imagine a robot arm with two segments. We adjust lengths x and y to reach a target point b in a 2D plane.

section_3.title: The Geometry of the Numerator
section_3.content: Explain Cramer's substitution. To solve for x, we replace column a1 with vector b. Geometrically, the determinant of this new matrix [b, a2] is the area of the parallelogram formed by b and a2. This area is equivalent to x times the area of the original [a1, a2] parallelogram due to the properties of linear transformations.
section_3.example: Show an animation where the parallelogram formed by [a1, a2] is 'stretched' and 'sheared' into the shape formed by [b, a2] as x changes.

section_4.title: Synthesis: The Ratio Formula
section_4.content: Conclude that x = Det(Ax) / Det(A). This is simply the ratio of the areas. If the area of the new shape is double the original, x must be 2. This intuition bridges the gap between algebraic manipulation and geometric scaling.
section_4.example: A scenario where a bird flying at vector b must decide its path relative to two wind vectors, with the 'area ratio' determining the required force.
